content.answer: Horace Danby was fifty years old, and everyone in the town thought he was a good, honest man — he ran a locksmith business, worked hard and was so gentle that he would never harm a fly. But the truth was that Horace was not really honest: he burgled a safe every year, stealing just enough to buy the rare, expensive books he loved. He had a perfect plan: he studied the family for a fortnight, knew their habits, and broke in only when the house would be empty. This year he had targeted the house of a rich man who lived in the country, a house with a safe containing precious stones.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The surprise in the house
content.answer: Horace got to the house as planned. He wore gloves and was careful not to leave fingerprints. Inside, he discovered a small safe that was easy to open — he had brought tools for a more difficult job. Just as he was opening the safe, a voice startled him: a young woman stood in the doorway, watching him. She said she was the wife of the rich man, and that she was too frightened to call the police because of her husband's temper — he would be very angry if he knew she was involved in a burglary. She asked Horace to open the safe and steal from it, but to give her all the money, and to leave her only with the jewels.

Horace, surprised by her calm, agreed. He opened the safe, took the jewels and handed them to her. She asked how he would escape the dog, and he explained his plan — the dog knew him because he had fed it on earlier visits. Before leaving, the woman asked him to tie her up and gag her, so that the police would believe she too was a victim. Horace did so, then escaped, pleased that he had done the job without violence. He even imagined the woman would keep his secret.

Three days later, Horace was arrested. The police had found his fingerprints in the house — on the door and on the safe. They showed him a photo of the real wife of the owner: she was a large, middle-aged woman, nothing like the young woman he had met. Horace realised he had been tricked. The young woman was another thief, who had simply appeared and taken the jewels. She had even stolen his gloves by playing on his kindness, asking him to tie her up so that his fingerprints would remain in the house. Horace, the "gentle" burglar who trusted a fellow thief, was caught because of that trust. He tells the police that the woman is a clever one — so clever that he would never tell anyone, not even to save himself, for he "could not describe her" — a quiet admission of his defeat.

The central theme is the irony of trust. Horace trusts the young woman's story completely — her claim to be the owner's wife, her fear of her husband's temper, her request for help — and that trust is his undoing. The title "A Question of Trust" is deeply ironic: the man whose profession is betrayal is himself betrayed, and the "gentle" thief is caught because he was too trusting of the wrong person.

The story illustrates that crime never pays, in the deepest sense. Horace's "harmless" yearly thefts — enough for his beloved books — lead him to a bigger job, where he is outwitted by a cleverer criminal and arrested. The story also shows that even the "gentle" criminal is a criminal: his trustworthiness, kindness and love of books do not excuse his burglaries, and in the end he pays for them.

Horace Danby is a fifty-year-old locksmith with an excellent reputation: the town believes him gentle, honest and hard-working. In truth he is a secret, methodical burglar who steals once a year, just enough to buy rare books — his one passion. He is careful, experienced and proud of his planning, yet he is also naive in a human way: he is moved by the young woman's story, treats her gallantly, and trusts her completely. That gallantry and trust are his downfall — he is betrayed, framed and arrested. Horace's tragedy is that his one genuinely good quality, trust, is exactly what destroys him. He remains a likeable figure, which makes the irony of his fate sharper.

The young woman is the brilliant villain of the story, a professional thief disguised as the rich man's wife. She is cool, quick-witted and utterly convincing: she appears in the doorway, plays on Horace's chivalry with her story of a violent husband, persuades him to open the safe, takes the jewels, asks him to tie her up — and even takes his gloves, telling him the dog would not know her scent. When the police come, they find only Horace's fingerprints. She vanishes without a trace, and Horace, impressed despite himself, refuses to describe her — "a clever one" indeed. She is the mirror image of Horace: a thief who trusts no one and wins.

content.prompt: The real wife and the police
content.answer: The real wife of the owner is a large, middle-aged woman whose photo in the newspaper shatters Horace's story. The police, efficient and thorough, discover Horace's fingerprints at the scene and piece together the truth: the young woman had taken his gloves, so his prints were everywhere, and the jewels were never recovered. The wife and the police represent the ordinary world that Horace's double life finally collides with — impersonal, patient and ultimately more successful than the cleverest burglar.

The story shows that a good reputation must be backed by true honesty. Horace was "good" in everyone's eyes yet lived a double life, and his secret crime destroyed him. The lesson is that character is what we do when no one is watching; trust is precious, and both giving and earning it require integrity.

The story also warns about misplaced trust. Horace's trust in the stranger was instant and complete, and it cost him his freedom. The lesson is not cynicism but discernment: kindness and gallantry are admirable, but they must be balanced with judgment, because not everyone who seems helpless deserves our confidence.

content.prompt: Why is the title "A Question of Trust" ironical?
content.answer: The title is deeply ironical because trust — an admirable quality — is exactly what destroys the burglar. Horace Danby is a criminal who trusts no one in his profession; he works alone, with careful plans and gloves. Yet when the young woman appears with her story, he trusts her completely: her claim to be the owner's wife, her fear of her husband's temper, her request for help. He even behaves gallantly, tying her up at her request. That trust is his undoing — she is a fellow thief who takes the jewels, takes his gloves and leaves his fingerprints behind. The "question of trust" is answered ironically: the man who trusted is arrested, and the woman who trusted no one escapes. Even at the end, Horace's trust is so complete that he refuses to describe her — he cannot bring himself to betray the person who betrayed him.

content.prompt: Describe the character of Horace Danby. Was he truly good?
content.answer: Horace Danby was fifty years old, a successful locksmith, gentle and hard-working, and universally considered honest — "he would not even harm a fly." But this goodness was a mask. Every year he planned and executed a burglary, stealing only enough to buy the rare books he loved. He was methodical, patient and proud of his skill, studying his targets for a fortnight. Yet his character had genuine softness: he was moved by the young woman's story, behaved with courtesy, and trusted her absolutely. He was not truly good — theft is theft, whatever the motive — but he was not truly bad either; he was a man with a weakness (books) and a self-deception (that his "gentle" crimes were harmless). The story shows that he paid for his double life: his one honest feeling, trust, became the trap that caught him.

content.prompt: How did the young woman outwit Horace?
content.answer: The young woman outwitted Horace at every step. First, she used psychology: instead of screaming or calling the police, she calmly announced herself as the owner's wife and gave a reason to stay silent — her husband's violent temper. This made Horace her accomplice instead of her enemy. Second, she made him do the work: he opened the safe and handed her the jewels, believing he was helping a frightened woman. Third, she secured the evidence: asking him to tie her up, she ensured his prints were on her and on the scene, and by taking his gloves she guaranteed his fingerprints would be found everywhere — while hers would not. Finally, she disappeared cleanly with the jewels, leaving Horace to the police. Her victory was total: she even persuaded him to admire her. Against her intelligence, Horace's careful planning was helpless.

content.prompt: Value question: What lesson does the story teach about trust and judgment?
content.answer: The story teaches that trust must be combined with judgment. Horace's downfall was not that he trusted, but that he trusted blindly and instantly — a stranger's story, told at midnight in a stolen house, was accepted without a question. The young woman exploited his gallantry and his belief in his own cleverness. The lesson is twofold. First, for the honest: our good qualities — kindness, trust, generosity — are precisely what dishonest people prey on, so they must be exercised with discernment. Second, for everyone: character is shown in what we do in secret; a reputation for honesty cannot survive a dishonest life. Horace's secret crimes were discovered, and his public goodness counted for nothing. The story's deepest message is that we should be trustworthy ourselves, and careful in whom we place our trust.

content.prompt: Why does Horace refuse to describe the young woman to the police?
content.answer: Horace's refusal to describe the young woman is the story's final irony. He tells the police that she was "a clever one" — and that he would never describe her, "not even to save himself." Several motives mingle here. There is grudging admiration: he respects her brilliance, and he is a professional himself. There is also wounded pride: she outwitted him completely, and describing her would be to admit that a simple story fooled him. And there may be a strange loyalty: in the strange morality of thieves, she was his companion in crime, and informing on her would be a final, unbearable humiliation. The refusal completes the title's irony — the victim of misplaced trust remains, to the end, trusting: he will not betray the one person who betrayed him.
